fit/gpu: Training runs on a GPU, short for graphics processing unit: a chip first built to draw graphics, which does thousands of multiplications at once. Everything training keeps must fit in its memory.
fit/bytes: Memory is counted in bytes. A bit is a single zero or one, and a byte is eight bits.
fit/gb: A billion bytes make a gigabyte, or G B, and a large GPU holds eighty of them.
fit/w: Take a model of seven billion parameters, each weight stored in sixteen bits: two bytes. Its weights take fourteen gigabytes. They fit, with room to spare.
fit/train: Yet training that same model with Adam needs more than this whole GPU. Where does the memory go?
param/one: Follow a single parameter. Its weight is a 16-bit number, sixteen zeros and ones: two bytes.
param/g: Each step computes its gradient, the slope that says which way to move it. That is also kept in 16 bits: two more bytes.
param/mix: Large models usually train with a mix. Sixteen bits for the numbers the arithmetic uses: they take half the memory, and a GPU computes with them faster. Thirty two bits, which take four bytes, for the optimizer's own numbers, which hold more digits.
param/master: So the optimizer keeps a 32-bit copy of every weight, called the master copy. Each step updates it, and the 16-bit weight is copied from it: four bytes.
param/mv: Then Adam's two running averages, m and v, also in 32 bits: four bytes each.
param/total: Two, plus two, plus four, plus four, plus four: sixteen bytes per parameter, called its training state. Only two of them are the weight the model computes with.
param/plain: Plain gradient descent keeps no running averages. Without m and v, it needs eight bytes.
model/n: Every parameter keeps its own sixteen bytes. Write N for the number of parameters: the model needs sixteen N bytes.
model/gb: For seven billion, sixteen times seven is a hundred and twelve: a hundred and twelve gigabytes.
model/gpu: One GPU holds eighty, so that is one point four GPUs' worth. A GPU does not come in parts, so round up: it takes two.
model/adam: In 2014, Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba wrote that Adam has little memory requirements, and per parameter it is little: m and v, eight bytes. But eight times seven billion is fifty six gigabytes, half the total.
model/big: Ten times the parameters is ten times the memory: a model of seventy billion parameters needs eleven hundred and twenty gigabytes.
model/many: At eighty per GPU, that is fourteen GPUs, just to hold the training state.
model/batch: Each step learns from a group of examples, called a batch. Its size never enters this count: one example or a thousand, each parameter keeps the same five numbers.
